questions.question_text:
A die is rolled $10$ times and these numbers come up:
$2, \; 4, \; 6, \; 4, \; 5, \; 1, \; 6, \; 4, \; 3, \; 3$
What is the relative frequency of rolling a $4$, as a fraction in simplest form?

options.why: This is the theoretical probability of rolling a $4$, not the relative frequency observed in these $10$ rolls.
Counts the $7$ rolls that were not a $4$ instead of the $3$ rolls that were.
Miscounts the frequency of $4$ as $4$; the number $4$ appears only $3$ times in the list.

questions.solution_text:
There are $10$ trials, and the number $4$ came up $3$ times.
$\text{Relative frequency} = \frac{3}{10}$

questions.question_text:
A coin is tossed $13$ times and these results come up:
$H, H, H, T, T, H, T, H, H, H, T, H, H$
What is the relative frequency of getting tails?

options.why: Counts the heads instead of the tails, giving the relative frequency of the other outcome over the $13$ trials.
Divides the $4$ tails by the $9$ heads instead of by the $13$ tosses, using the count of the other outcome as the denominator.
Writes the odds of heads to tails, $9$ to $4$, instead of a relative frequency out of the total number of tosses.

questions.solution_text:
There are $13$ trials, and tails came up $4$ times.
$\text{Relative frequency} = \frac{4}{13}$

questions.question_text: When a coin is tossed $100$ times, the results are $53$ heads and $47$ tails. What is the relative frequency of getting a head, as a decimal?

options.why: This is the relative frequency of tails, not heads.
This is the theoretical probability of heads, not the relative frequency observed in these $100$ tosses.
This is the frequency of heads; the relative frequency divides it by the $100$ trials.

questions.question_text:
A die is rolled $40$ times and the results are recorded in the table.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Outcome} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\\hline \text{Frequency} & 5 & 7 & 6 & 9 & 5 & 8 \\\hline \end{array}$
What is the relative frequency of rolling a $2$, as a fraction in simplest form?

options.why: Reads the frequency $9$ from the outcome $4$ column instead of the frequency $7$ from the outcome $2$ column.
Divides the $7$ twos by the $33$ rolls that were not a $2$, since $40-7=33$, instead of by all $40$ trials.
Reads the outcome $4$ column and then divides by the $31$ rolls that were not a $4$, since $40-9=31$, instead of by all $40$ trials.

questions.solution_text:
There are $40$ trials, and the number $2$ came up $7$ times.
$\text{Relative frequency} = \frac{7}{40}$

questions.question_text: A die is rolled $10$ times and the number $3$ comes up $4$ times. If the same experiment were repeated with $600$ trials, what would you expect the frequency of $3$ to be?

options.why: Uses the theoretical probability $\frac{1}{6}$ instead of the observed relative frequency $\frac{4}{10}$.
Keeps the frequency from the $10$ rolls without scaling it up to $600$ trials.
Divides the trials by $10$ instead of multiplying the relative frequency $\frac{4}{10}$ by $600$.

questions.question_text: A drawing pin is tossed $200$ times and lands point-up $130$ times. What is the best estimate of the probability that the pin lands point-up, as a decimal?

options.why: Assumes point-up and point-down are equally likely, but the pin is not symmetric, so the observed results must be used.
This estimates the probability of landing point-down, not point-up.
Divides $130$ by $1000$ instead of by the $200$ trials, misplacing the decimal point.

questions.solution_text:
The pin is not symmetric, so the observed probability is the best estimate.
$\text{Observed probability} = \frac{130}{200}$
$= 0.65$

questions.question_text: Mia rolls a fair die $15$ times, and Noah rolls the same die $600$ times. Each of them calculates the relative frequency of rolling a six. Whose relative frequency would you expect to be closer to the theoretical probability of rolling a six?

options.why: Fewer trials give relative frequencies that can be far from the theoretical probability.
The Law of Large Numbers says more trials bring the relative frequency closer to the theoretical probability, so the two experiments differ.

options.text: It is impossible to say anything about them
options.why: Any single result varies, but the Law of Large Numbers still makes the larger experiment the better bet for a closer relative frequency.

questions.solution_text:
By the Law of Large Numbers, as the number of trials increases, the relative frequency approaches the theoretical probability.
Noah rolls the die far more times, so his relative frequency is expected to be closer to $\frac{1}{6}$.

options.why: Reads the relative frequency after only $10$ flips; with few trials the relative frequency can be far from the true probability.
Assumes top-up and top-down are equally likely, but a bottle top is not symmetric, so the graph's settled value must be used.

questions.solution_text:
The relative frequency jumps around at first, then settles closer and closer to $0.4$ as the number of flips increases.
By the Law of Large Numbers, this settled value is the best estimate.
$P(\text{top-up}) \approx 0.4$

questions.question_text:
A die was rolled $60$ times. The results are shown in the table.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Outcome} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\\hline \text{Frequency} & 12 & 8 & A & 9 & 11 & 13 \\\hline \end{array}$
What is the relative frequency of rolling a $3$, as a fraction in simplest form?

options.why: This is the theoretical probability of rolling a $3$; the question asks for the relative frequency, using $A = 7$.
Uses the frequency of $4$, which is $9$, instead of first finding $A = 7$ for the number $3$.
Divides $A = 7$ by the other $53$ rolls instead of by all $60$ trials.
